# What we built

## What composable modelling would need

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Uncertainty and inference.** Propagate it properly; swap the
  inference method
- **Model structure.** Separate infection, latent, and observation
  processes; nest models inside models
- **Population heterogeneity.** Stratify any component without hand
  managing the bookkeeping
- **Accessibility and interoperability.** Components carry their priors,
  work standalone, and talk to the rest of Julia
- **Workflow.** One specification for simulation and for inference
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
## Composable modelling
Components can be validated on their own, then combined in
configurations nobody planned for, without losing rigour.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
These came from the authors and have had no community input.
:::

::: {.attribution}
Table 1 of the paper. Six themes, each requirement paired with the
problem that motivates it.
:::
:::
::::

## The proof of concept

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- A thin language for epidemiology over a probabilistic backend that
  does the sampling
- Three component families. Infection, latent, and observation
  processes, composing across families as well as within them
- Components carry their own priors, so domain knowledge travels with
  the component rather than with the person
- Model definitions do not know about the data, so one definition
  simulates and fits
- An R interface, so choosing Julia is not a wall for the people who
  would use it

::: {.attribution}
Abbott et al., *Composable probabilistic models can lower barriers to
rigorous infectious disease modelling*,
[doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17884675](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17884675)
:::
